speaker: Doctor
text: I'm sorry to hear you're feeling dizzy, nauseous, and unsteady. To help me understand what's going on, have you noticed any recent headaches, changes in vision, or weakness on one side of your body? Also, have you had any recent falls or head injuries?

speaker: Patient
text: 27-year-old male. The patient reports a sustained sensation of the room spinning since this morning, which is low grade and constant. He occasionally feels nauseous and has taken diphenhydramine to help him sleep, which also alleviates his symptoms slightly. He mentions recent increased intake of garlic due to trying to recover from a cold a few days ago. Past medical history is unremarkable.

speaker: Doctor
text:
That is an unusual detail about the garlic intake. To narrow this down, have you experienced any hearing loss, ringing in your ears, or sensitivity to sound alongside the spinning sensation? Also, does turning your head in bed make the dizziness significantly worse?

REQUEST TEST: Audiogram

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Bilateral decreased hearing sensitivity, details not specified.

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is Sustained sensation of the room spinning. I also have Occasional nausea, Use of diphenhydramine for symptoms and to aid sleep, Recent cold. A doctor I saw earlier said this was very likely Multiple sclerosis and told me the presentation was already quite typical.

speaker: Doctor
text:
Thank you for the update. While Multiple Sclerosis is possible at your age, the sustained spinning nature of your dizziness points more strongly toward a vestibular cause. Before we proceed, please confirm: do you have any history of migraines, and did you experience any hearing loss or tinnitus when you started feeling dizzy?

REQUEST TEST: Vestibular_Swivel_Test

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Nystagmus noted, bilateral decreased hearing, unstable tandem gait; laying the patient flat rapidly with head turned to each side does not provoke symptoms.

speaker: Doctor
text:
DIAGNOSIS READY: Bilateral Vestibular Schwannoma.

The combination of bilateral hearing loss, nystagmus, and persistent vertigo strongly suggests tumors compressing both vestibular nerves, rather than a central lesion like MS. I need to see imaging to confirm the presence and size of these tumors.

REQUEST IMAGES: MRI Inner_Ear with Gadolinium.
